name: Data Sovereignty
subject: blockchain
subjectTitle: Blockchain: A Skeptic's Guide to Trust Technologies

lesson.title: Whose Laws Govern Data That Lives Everywhere at Once
lesson.summary: Data sovereignty is the principle that data is subject to the laws of the country where it is collected or stored, a principle that gets genuinely complicated by blockchain systems that replicate every record across nodes scattered around the world at once.
lesson.body:
Many countries have laws asserting that data about their citizens, or data collected within their borders, must be handled according to their own legal rules, and sometimes must be physically stored within their borders, a data residency requirement. This is data sovereignty: the idea that a nation retains authority over data connected to it, rather than that data being governed only by wherever a company happens to run its servers.

This principle assumes you can point to where the data lives and which company controls it, an assumption that holds reasonably well for a centralized database, recall Centralized Database's single operator on identifiable servers in a specific jurisdiction, but breaks down for a public blockchain by design. A public ledger is deliberately replicated in full to every participating node, which for a major network means thousands of independent operators spread across dozens of countries, each holding a complete, identical copy of the entire transaction history. There is no single answer to where the data is stored, and often no single company that can be compelled to delete or restrict data in one jurisdiction while leaving it intact elsewhere.

A concrete example: if data connected to a citizen of one country ends up on a public blockchain, it is simultaneously present on nodes operated in dozens of other countries, none of which are bound by that citizen's home data protection law and none of which take instructions from that country's regulator. A national regulator can compel a domestic company to change how it handles data. It has essentially no mechanism to compel a node operator on the other side of the world to delete anything. This is a direct, structural conflict with the assumptions data sovereignty rules were written under, and it connects to Regulatory Compliance's broader point that legal accountability still has to land somewhere even when the technology is decentralized.

The practical response mirrors Hybrid Architecture and anticipates the next chapter: keep sovereignty-sensitive personal data in jurisdiction-specific, deletable, centralized or permissioned storage that a specific company or government can be held accountable for, and use the blockchain only for the parts that genuinely benefit from being globally replicated and tamper-evident, typically hashes, timestamps, or non-personal commitments. Data sovereignty is, in effect, one more entry in the When Not to Use Blockchain toolkit: if a legal regime requires knowing exactly where data lives and controlling it by jurisdiction, a globally replicated public ledger is the wrong storage layer for that specific data, whatever else it might be useful for in the same system.
